catalog_quote: [Ribeiro 2006:19, 'Phonology'] The primary stress falls ordinarily on the last syllable of a stem (4a). Secondary stress is generally assigned on an iambic, right-to-left pattern to every other syllable (4b). [(4a) wa-riOrE 1-child 'my child'; (4b) wa-riOrE-riOrE 1-child-child 'my grandchild'] As the examples show, in order to fit the iambic pattern, the original stress pattern of a stem may be rearranged under compounding (4b), as well as under suffixation, since all derivational suffixes are stressed. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and final within the stem/derived word: primary stress on the last syllable of the stem (derivational suffixes count as part of the stressed domain and take the stress), with enclitics (tense-aspect markers, indefinite article, most postpositions) outside the stress domain; secondary stresses alternate leftward from the primary (iambic, right-to-left). Corroborated in Portuguese by Ribeiro 2001/2002 p.76: 'A posição do acento é predizível, recaindo geralmente sobre a última sílaba da palavra' and p.80 'acento fixo na última sílaba'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress is generally assigned on an iambic, right-to-left pattern to every other syllable' (p.19), e.g. wa-riore-riore [ˌwariˌoreˌrioˈre] 'my grandchild'.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Tense-aspect clitics, the indefinite article and most postpositions are unstressed, but 'become stressed when attached to monosyllabic stems' (p.23 fn.6: he=di 'with firewood' [heˈdi], r-a=kre 'he will go' [raˈkre]); the imperfective =r-e becomes stressed before the future marker. (ii) Grammatical 'stress shift': in relative/subordinate clauses stress moves from the stem-final syllable onto the tense-aspect clitic (p.18: [doroˈde] 'the White man who arrived' vs [doˈrode] 'the White man arrived'), the basic marker of subordination.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem plus derivational suffixes (the 'phonological word characterized by a single primary stress', Ribeiro 2002: 481); enclitics are extrametrical except after monosyllabic hosts and under subordination stress shift. Ribeiro 2001/2002 phrases the same generalization at word level ('última sílaba da palavra'). Examples are given in phonetic transcription of words/short phrases; female-speech forms are the citation standard.
new_statements.identity_note: Ribeiro's statements cover Karajá as a whole (four dialects: Southern Karajá, Northern Karajá, Javaé, Xambioá; he notes they 'share basically the same phonological system'); his examples are mainly Southern/Northern Karajá female speech. Glottolog kara1500 = the language-level node; Javaé (java1245) and Xambioá are dialects under it.

sources.note: p.19 'Phonology': primary stress ordinarily on the last syllable of a stem; secondary stress iambic right-to-left on every other syllable; all derivational suffixes stressed; tense-aspect clitics, indefinite article and most postpositions unstressed (fn.6 p.23: they get stress after monosyllabic stems); p.18/§ on relativization: stress shifts from stem-final syllable to the tense-aspect clitic to mark relative/subordinate clauses.
